documents: Guan et al. (2022) Geophysical Research Letters 49, e2022GL098549, published paper (PDF, 9 pages); Supporting Information S1 not supplied
pages_convention: PDF pages counted from 1 (these match the printed 'n of 9' page labels)

entry.evidence: The S-wave polarization anisotropy and azimuthal anisotropy were widely observed near the subducting slabs in the lower part of the mantle transition zone (MTZ) ... [...]

sequences.source_document: Guan et al. 2022, GRL, published PDF

steps.action: The authors take from seismological studies that polarization and azimuthal anisotropy are seen near subducting slabs in the lower MTZ.
steps.quote: were widely observed near the subducting slabs in the lower part of the mantle transition zone (MTZ)

steps.action: The authors pose the open question of the origin of the lower-MTZ anisotropy.
steps.quote: while the origin remains unclear and is still under debate

steps.action: From published elasticity and phase-equilibria work, the authors set aside ringwoodite, majorite, CaSiO3 perovskite, wadsleyite and bridgmanite as the main source of the anisotropy.
steps.quote: which contributes little to the observed seismic anisotropy

steps.action: The authors propose LPO of elastically anisotropic akimotoite, stable near cold slabs at 21-24 GPa, as the candidate source.
steps.quote: Thus, the LPO of akimotoite might be the strong candidate for the origin of the observed seismic anisotropies

steps.action: The authors note that the akimotoite slip system is disputed between Shiraishi et al. (2008) and Cordier (2002), so its LPO is unknown.
steps.quote: Therefore, the slip system of akimotoite is still controversial.

steps.action: The authors adopt the D111-type Kawai-type apparatus with differential rams (Hunt et al. 2014), which decouples deformation from pressure generation.
steps.quote: It decouples the deformation from the pressure generation and enables us to deform the sample under a well-controlled strain rate

steps.action: The authors synthesized akimotoite aggregates from glass and checked them by XRD, SEM and EBSD as well-sintered, equigranular, about 10 μm, with random lattice orientations.
steps.quote: Analysis results show that samples were well-sintered akimotoite aggregates with equigranular texture

steps.action: The authors ran uniaxial and shear deformation experiments at 21-23 GPa and 900-1300°C, with 20 min annealing and a constant d-ram displacement rate of 1-2 µm/min.
steps.quote: we used the well-sintered akimotoite aggregates as starting materials for deformation experiments performed at 21–23 GPa and 900–1300°C

steps.action: The authors measured lattice orientations of recovered samples by EBSD and by transmitted 2D synchrotron X-ray diffraction (SPring-8 BL04B1), combining two incident directions.
steps.quote: we measured the lattice orientation of recovered samples by using EBSD and transmitted two-dimensional (2D) X-ray diffraction method

steps.action: The authors checked that EBSD and 2D XRD give similar LPO patterns on the same deformed sample.
steps.quote: that the obtained LPO patterns were similar by using the EBSD and the 2D X-ray diffraction technique for the same deformed sample

steps.action: The authors measured water contents by FT-IR (Paterson 1982), found them low (at most 42 ± 16 wt ppm) against hydrous akimotoite, and judged them consistent with a dry MTZ.
steps.quote: Compared with the hydrous akimotoite (Bolfan-Casanova et al., 2000; Ye et al., 2013), the water contents in our samples were quite low.

steps.action: The authors observed porphyroclastic textures with recrystallized grains in deformed samples, which they read as dislocation creep.
steps.quote: suggesting that the dynamic recrystallization occurred during deformation and that the dislocation creep would be the dominant deformation mechanism

steps.action: The authors used a sample annealed in the shear cell without d-ram advance as a control; its strain marker shows no deformation during compression and heating.
steps.quote: indicating almost no deformation during compression and heating

steps.action: The authors computed shear strain and average shear strain rate from strain-marker rotation and deformation time (Table S1).
steps.quote: From the rotation angle of the strain marker and the deformation time, the shear strain and average shear strain rate could be calculated

steps.action: The authors described the LPO patterns: [0001] parallel to compression in uniaxial runs and normal to the shear plane in shear runs, with the shear direction preferring the <10-10> axis at γ = 2.1.
steps.quote: the [0001] axis was preferentially aligned to the direction perpendicular to the shear plane

steps.action: The authors compared fabrics across temperatures (900-1200°C uniaxial; 1000-1300°C shear) and deformation geometries and found no change.
steps.quote: The deformation fabrics do not change between temperatures within 900–1200°C.

steps.action: The authors inferred from the LPO that the dominant slip system is <10-10>(0001), with no change between 900 and 1300°C.
steps.quote: Based on the observation of Figure 2 and S4 in Supporting Information S1, we conclude that the most dominant slip system of akimotoite

steps.action: The authors computed aggregate elastic constants and seismic anisotropy from measured LPO and single-crystal constants (Li et al. 2009, Mainprice 1990 software): P 2.5%, S 1.98%, VSH > VSV for horizontal shearing, AVSH 1.22% and AVSV 1.96%.
steps.quote: We estimated the elastic wave velocities of shear-deformed samples based on the LPO data in the present study

steps.action: The authors compared their slip system with the stress-relaxation results of Shiraishi et al. (2008) and Cordier (2002) and found both inconsistent.
steps.quote: The result of Shiraishi et al. (2008) at low temperature is inconsistent with that in the present study.

steps.action: The authors rejected water content as the cause of the discrepancy, since Shiraishi's starting sample was similarly dry (24 wt ppm).
steps.quote: This contradiction may not be caused by [...]

steps.action: The authors propose that uncontrolled or abnormal stress in stress-relaxation experiments explains the earlier slip-system results.
steps.quote: The discrepancy between both previous studies and our study might result from the different stress conditions.

steps.action: The authors computed polarization anisotropy of a pyrolitic aggregate (60% ringwoodite, 20% pyrope, 20% akimotoite) along a 1300°C geotherm, using Voigt, Reuss and VRH averages.
steps.quote: we estimated the seismic anisotropies of rock aggregate of pyrolitic composition with 60 vol.% ringwoodite, 20 vol.% iron-bearing pyrope, and 20 vol.% akimotoite

steps.action: The authors checked that VSH²/VSV² differs negligibly between the Voigt and Reuss averages, which justifies using VRH.
steps.quote: shows a negligibly small difference between Voigt and Reuss averages

steps.action: The authors compared computed VSH²/VSV² with observed values near slabs (Ferreira et al. 2019) sorted by slab geometry: horizontal shearing matches stagnant and shallow slabs, vertical shearing at γ = 2.1 matches steep slabs.
steps.quote: are consistent with that observed beneath most of the stagnant and shallowly penetrating slabs

steps.action: For West Java, where observed anisotropy is stronger than predicted, the authors invoke a larger akimotoite volume fraction or shear strain rather than revising the hypothesis.
steps.quote: indicating that a larger volume fraction or shear strain (larger than γ = 2.1) of akimotoite may exist in that region

steps.action: The authors extended the explanation to other observations: the two Tonga slab segments, stronger anisotropy near older slabs, and stronger azimuthal anisotropy in the circum-Pacific than the central Pacific (Huang et al. 2019).
steps.quote: can be interpreted by the LPO of different amount of akimotoite

steps.action: The authors keep the claim that akimotoite LPO can explain or contribute to the lower-MTZ anisotropy near slabs.
steps.quote: It is considered that the LPO of akimotoite could contribute to the observed azimuthal anisotropy near the subducting slabs.

tree.answer: Polarization and azimuthal anisotropy near slabs in the lower MTZ, from cited seismology
No; the mineral source is latent, so LPO is reproduced in laboratory analogues
Explain the origin of the anisotropy; resolve the akimotoite slip system
Other MTZ minerals set aside by citation; rival slip systems from Shiraishi 2008 and Cordier 2002
Computed VSH/VSV from LPO for horizontal versus vertical shearing, against weakly anisotropic ringwoodite
Set: controlled-strain-rate deformation at 21-23 GPa and 900-1300°C

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Nature repeats across slabs of differing geometry and age (Ferreira 2019, Huang 2019, Tonga)
Fabric stable across temperature and geometry; EBSD and XRD agree; Voigt and Reuss differences negligible
Kept: akimotoite LPO can explain the observed anisotropy (best explanation)
No review file supplied; acknowledgments mention two anonymous reviewers

end.claim: The lattice preferred orientation of akimotoite, with dominant slip <10-10>(0001), produces strong polarization and azimuthal anisotropy (VSH > VSV for horizontal shearing) that can explain the seismic anisotropy observed near subducting slabs in the lower MTZ.

decisive_move.sentence: The constant-strain-rate shear deformation experiments in the D111 Kawai-type apparatus at lower-MTZ conditions produced the measured LPO, and every later anisotropy calculation and comparison rests on it.

gates.evidence: The akimotoite-LPO hypothesis (p. 2) set the experimental conditions near cold-slab P-T. The predicted VSH²/VSV² could have mismatched observations, but the West Java mismatch was absorbed by an unconstrained volume fraction or strain (p. 6). No analysis or threshold was fixed in advance.

imports.item: electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) for lattice orientation
transmitted 2D monochromatic X-ray diffraction at SPring-8 BL04B1, analysed with ReciPro
Voigt, Reuss and Voigt-Reuss-Hill averaging of elastic tensors
ab initio single-crystal elastic constants of akimotoite (Li et al. 2009)

limits: No review file was supplied, so nothing of the review process is coded. Supporting Information S1 (Table S1, Figures S1-S6, Texts S1-S2) was not supplied; steps resting on it are coded from main-text statements only. Rival mineral sources (ringwoodite, majorite, CaSiO3 perovskite) are excluded only by citation, not tested here. The slip-system sub-claim (<10-10>(0001) across 900-1300°C) is at regularity_in_range, from few runs; small-strain samples show no clear shear-direction preference, so the inference rests mainly on one large-strain run (γ = 2.1, D056). The stress-condition explanation of the disagreement with Shiraishi 2008 and Cordier 2002 is proposed, not tested. Stress was not measured, so dislocation creep is inferred from microstructure. Samples are Fe-free MgSiO3, while the natural phase is (Mg,Fe)SiO3. The match to observations depends on assumed volume fraction (20%) and strain, which are adjusted ad hoc for West Java; inference: this weakens the claim gate. Composition coded none_fits: a hypothesis-led laboratory experiment followed by a forward calculation compared with seismological traces, with no shared crucial test among rivals.

disagreements.target: Shiraishi et al. (2008), slip system change at ~1100°C with [0001] slip at 1000°C
disagreements.support: Constant-strain-rate D111 experiments show <10-10>(0001) with no change from 900 to 1300°C; water content is ruled out as the cause because both studies used dry samples.
disagreements.quote: The result of Shiraishi et al. (2008) at low temperature is inconsistent with that in the present study.

disagreements.support: The shear-direction concentration at large strain prefers <10-10> over <11-20>.
disagreements.quote: slip direction is in contradiction with our results

disagreements.target: Stress-relaxation deformation experiments in Kawai-type multianvil apparatus
disagreements.support: The authors argue from cited work (Nishihara et al. 2010, 2020) that deviatoric stress in stress relaxation is uncontrollable and abnormal at low temperature; no direct test is made here.
disagreements.quote: [...] -relaxation experiment, the magnitude of deviatoric stress was uncontrollable and complicated, especially at low-temperature ranges

alternatives_considered.reason: High-quality Kikuchi bands were hard to obtain because of large lattice distortion

alternatives_considered.chosen: Single-crystal elastic constants at 20.6 GPa and 1227°C for all conditions
alternatives_considered.reason: Temperature effects on elastic constants are negligibly small in the experimental range
